title: Pay off debt with interest rates above your expected real return
summary: Operationally: anything above ~6–7% after-tax. Credit cards (15–28%), payday loans (300%+), private student loans (often 8–14%) — these are guaranteed-loss positions you can close.
detailsHtml:
The threshold logic

The right threshold is not a fixed number like the original chart's 10% — it is the rate above your expected after-tax real return on alternative investments. If your taxable brokerage account is expected to return ~5% real after taxes, debt above 5% should be prioritized; the comparison is rate-versus-rate, not rate-versus-zero.

Decision rule: Debt rate > (expected investment return × (1 − marginal tax rate)) → pay down debt first Example: 22% bracket, 7% expected nominal return 7% × (1 − 0.22) = 5.46% after-tax Debt above ~5.5% should be prepaid Debt below that can be deferred while you invest

Avalanche vs. snowball

The avalanche method (pay highest rate first) minimizes total interest paid — mathematically optimal. The snowball method (pay smallest balance first) builds psychological momentum through quick wins — behaviorally optimal for many people. The right choice depends on your honest assessment of your discipline.

Empirically, Northwestern's Kellogg research has found that people on snowball plans complete their payoffs at higher rates than people on avalanche plans, even though avalanche is cheaper per dollar. Completion is the dominant variable; pick the method you'll actually finish.

Federal student loans are an exception. They have features civilian debt doesn't: income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, deferment options. If you're pursuing PSLF, aggressively paying down federal loans is mathematically wrong — you should pay the minimum on IDR and maximize forgiveness.
